1: Lead a new hire through the roof layers from deck to ridge. Name each layer in order and explain its role with natural Japanese sequencing such as まず and 次に.
2: Explain to a new hire how water travels across the roof, why joints are staggered to the manufacturer's pattern, and what can happen over time if they line up.
3: Coach a new crew member on nail placement and depth. Show the nailing zone, correct high and overdriven nails with clear Japanese requests, and keep a supportive tone.
4: Read the relevant manufacturer instructions before installing flashing. Explain the order, specified fasteners and overlap, and confirm that the crew will follow the sheet.
5: Tell the homeowner about rotten deck found during tear-off. Show the photos, explain the proposed repair, added cost and time, and request authorization on the change order politely.
6: Ask the supplier what is missing and when it may arrive. Compare the proposed substitute with the contracted product, request its specification, and explain the approval and delivery plan.
7: Walk an insurance adjuster through the observed hail marks. Give the storm time, test-square location, counts and measurements clearly, then discuss the proposed scope of work.
8: Respond to a homeowner who asks the crew to work during a storm and omit underlayment. Decline both requests politely and directly, explain why the crew will not do either, and offer the tarp-and-return alternative.
9: Speak privately with a worker about a crooked course. Ask what happened, describe the exposure and alignment, request a specific measurement-based correction, and confirm the plan.
10: Hear each crew member's account of the loose tarp, report their statements accurately to the boss, and set a fair tie-down check and assignment for the next shift.
11: Acknowledge a difficult heat-wave week, explain the changed hours, water and shade breaks, and use the direct terms for dizziness, heat exhaustion and heatstroke when discussing the crew's plan.
13: Report a worker's fall to the supervisor in time order. State what happened, the observed injury, the call for help, and what the incident report will record without inventing an exact time.
14: Discuss a falling-bundle near-miss with the crew. Describe what happened and what could have happened, invite the worker's account, and agree on a concrete prevention change without assigning blame.
15: Use short, clear Japanese radio calls to announce the storm alert, assign tarp and loose-material tasks, confirm receipt, and direct the crew down when thunder is heard.
16: Greet the city inspector politely, present the permit, explain the observed fastening and flashing method, ask for the exact correction, and state the re-inspection plan.
17: Give the office manager a concise end-of-day report with hours, roofing squares completed, rotten-deck repair, materials used, photo evidence and open items. Use Japanese report connectors naturally.
18: Answer a homeowner's return call about the rain delay, propose a new day and arrival time politely, recover from the dropped call, and confirm the revised appointment in writing.
19: Walk the homeowner through the completed work and the two source-scenario warranties. Explain the stated coverage, exclusions, contact path and final-invoice questions in clear polite Japanese.
20: Lead the storm-repair day in Japanese: brief the crew, walk the adjuster through the damage, explain the deck repair and change order, respond to the near-miss and weather, and give an end-of-day report.
